title: The Houthis seize the second strait, and $100 oil is just the start
dek: Red Sea shipping volumes have already halved from their peak and never recovered, and now the Houthis have taken Perim Island in the Bab-el-Mandeb, putting Saudi Arabia's alternative export route around Hormuz in doubt too.
why: Eight minutes to explain why a strait most people have never heard of suddenly matters, with concrete mechanics and numbers — good for a commute.
who: Investors and founders watching geopolitical risk, commodities and supply chains, especially anyone who needs to judge where oil prices, freight rates and insurance costs are heading.
skip: The two opening teaser segments and the podcast promo at the end can be skipped.

points.h: The Red Sea is not just another waterway
points.body: In normal, calm times, nearly 15% of global seaborne trade passes through the Red Sea, including 30% of global container shipping, 12% of seaborne oil trade and 8% of liquefied natural gas. At its northern end the Red Sea connects to Egypt and the Suez Canal, and on to the Mediterranean; at its southern end that narrow channel leading to the Indian Ocean and Asian trade routes is the Bab-el-Mandeb. To grasp the weight of this strait, you first have to grasp how much the Red Sea itself carries — it is not a bypass you can casually route around, but a stretch of the global trade trunk road.

points.h: The Houthis really did take that ground
points.body: The host pressed Rachel on whether "seem to have seized" was hedging, and Rachel confirmed it: the Houthis are a rebel group that has been gradually taking control of large parts of Yemen since at least 2014, allied with Iran, and strongly opposed to Israel's existence and to how Israel is fighting in Gaza. In November 2023 they began attacking Red Sea shipping, hijacking vessels and striking with drones and missiles; the US military responded with bombing, and the Red Sea was relatively calm for a while. But over the weekend they moved, seizing a stretch of Yemen's Red Sea coast, possibly to support Iran.

points.h: Perim Island is the key that pinches the strait
points.body: The seized stretch includes an island right in the middle of the Bab-el-Mandeb — Perim Island (Barim Island), which the military calls "key terrain" because it overlooks the entire strait, and the strait is only about 18 miles wide at its narrowest point. Whoever controls that chokepoint decides which ships can pass. Red Sea traffic had already slowed because of the Houthi attacks, initially falling 50%, and it never fully recovered. Now that Perim Island has been taken, the threat is that this route shuts down entirely.

points.h: Saudi Arabia's way around Hormuz is now in doubt too
points.body: This is a particularly thorny problem for Saudi Arabia. After Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz more than six months ago, Saudi Arabia had been treating the Red Sea and the Bab-el-Mandeb as an alternative oil export route, sending oil through an east-west pipeline to Red Sea ports for loading. But last week that Saudi Red Sea pipeline was hit by a drone attack, and Saudi Arabia then suspended oil loadings from one Red Sea port. Rachel says this puts even more pressure on this lifeline for Saudi Arabia and for the global economy — the creative workaround meant to cushion the world economy is itself extremely fragile.

points.h: Schrodinger Strait: collecting the toll without firing a shot
points.body: The Houthis could close the Bab-el-Mandeb at any time, but so far they haven't. Rachel says the mere fact that they can is already having an effect. Analysts call it the "Schrodinger Strait" — is it open or closed? That uncertainty alone pushes up insurance costs and freight rates, adding friction to the global economy. After news of the Houthi advance last week, oil prices briefly spiked above $100 a barrel.

points.h: Refined products are rising faster than crude
points.body: Rachel points out that timing is crucial: the global supply gap was already building, only partly offset by rerouting and releases from strategic petroleum reserves, while refineries have seen serious outages. That means not only are crude prices up, but diesel, gasoline and other petroleum products are rising by proportionally more, because getting refined products to market has become harder. And it isn't just oil products — this strait also carries fertilizer and natural gas, which would be a problem if Europe has a cold winter.

points.h: Sulfur and helium: the overlooked knock-on shortages
points.body: Sulfur is a byproduct of natural gas and fuel production, its supply is already more constrained, and it is used in metal processing, including copper. Helium is a byproduct of natural gas deposits, used as an input in semiconductors and in all kinds of medical equipment. Countries like the US and Canada are ramping up production of some of these goods, offsetting some of the price increases, but Rachel says not by much. That means shortages from this new trade disruption will reach ordinary people before long.

points.h: American consumers end up footing the bill
points.body: Rachel says Americans should care because these are global markets, and you can't build a wall to stop imports. Some US producers may benefit from shortages, but in this kind of scenario American consumers tend to be the ones who lose. She also warns that it isn't just higher prices to worry about: the Houthi actions, plus Iran's refusal to yield, are straining relations among regional countries and between the US and its Middle East allies. Deteriorating relations between the US and its allies could make other US policy goals harder to achieve — Gulf states, for instance, are major investors in the US and key to US onshore production.
